title: Making supermarkets give away unsold food

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: France made it illegal for big supermarkets to bin unsold food. They have to have an agreement with a charity. That was two thousand sixteen.

turns.speaker: Callum
turns.text: And did it work? Because a law can pass and change almost nothing.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Donations went up a lot. The tonnage roughly doubled in the first few years.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: Doubled in weight, though. That's the number I'd look at twice. If what you double is bread and bruised fruit, the food banks now have a logistics problem instead of an empty shelf.

turns.speaker: Callum
turns.text: Yes, somebody has to collect it, chill it and move it the same day.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: And that somebody is usually a volunteer with a car.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: The French law did fund some of that, to be fair. Not all of it.

turns.speaker: Callum
turns.text: The thing I keep coming back to is that it treats the symptom. You're at the end of the chain, moving surplus around. Nobody's asking why the surplus is that size.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Because forecasting a supermarket is hard and empty shelves cost them more than waste does.

turns.speaker: Callum
turns.text: Right, so the incentive is to over-order. Until that changes, you're just deciding where the excess goes.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: Which is still better than a skip.

turns.speaker: Callum
turns.text: Oh, much better. I'm not arguing against it. I'm arguing against calling it a solution.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: That's a distinction I can live with.

points: France banned large supermarkets from binning unsold food in 2016, requiring agreements with charities.
Donations roughly doubled by weight in the first few years.
Noor questions the weight measure: doubling low-value items creates a logistics burden for food banks rather than solving hunger.
Collection, chilling and same-day transport typically fall on volunteers, though the French law funded some of it.
Callum's main objection is that the law treats a symptom at the end of the chain without addressing why the surplus exists.
Rosa explains the incentive: empty shelves cost supermarkets more than waste, so they over-order. They agree the policy is better than landfill but should not be called a solution.
